hero.badge: BUILT FOR HOW LEBANON ACTUALLY TALKS
hero.subtitle: My Hayat is a Lebanese-first mental-health support AI built around Arabizi, local context, and a safety-first conversation design. Talk in English, Arabic, or the mix in between — My Hayat helps you understand patterns, learn practical tools, and find a useful next step.
features.zeroJudgment.title: Lebanese, not translated
features.zeroJudgment.desc: A dedicated Lebanese Arabizi layer handles spelling, code-switching, gender and person agreement, and local phrasing that generic Arabic models miss.
features.dialect.title: Built to help you move forward
features.dialect.desc: My Hayat is not optimized to keep a conversation going forever. Its job is to help you understand what is happening, build skills, and reconnect with your own decisions.
features.247.title: Safety before fluency
features.247.desc: High-risk language is handled deterministically before the model generates. Ordinary replies are checked before display for dialect failures, script mismatches, and reasoning leaks — with retry and conservative fallback when needed.
echoes.title: Patterns are easier to see when they stop
echoes.desc: Echoes is the reflection layer in the My Hayat roadmap: a way to notice recurring themes, moods, and habits across time without turning your private life into a scoreboard.

about.hero.title: Mental-health AI has a language problem.
about.hero.titleHighlight: In Lebanon, that becomes an access problem.
about.hero.subtitle: My Hayat started with a simple observation: support is less useful when people have to translate themselves before they can ask for it.
about.crisis.title: The context
about.crisis.stat1.label: of economic instability, conflict, and repeated shocks to the health system
about.crisis.stat2.label: barriers — cost, availability, stigma, privacy — that make formal care difficult to access
about.crisis.stat3.label: language that Lebanese people actually use: a mix of Arabic, English, French, and Arabizi
about.crisis.stat4.label: existing AI systems built specifically for how Lebanese people actually talk and think
about.crisis.desc: Lebanon's mental-health burden sits on top of years of economic instability, conflict, displacement, and strain on the health system. Formal care also has practical barriers: cost, availability, privacy, stigma, and the fear — still real in many families — that asking for psychological help means weakness or illness. My Hayat is not a substitute for fixing those systems. It is an attempt to make one layer of support easier to reach.
about.mission.title: What we're building
about.mission.desc: A Lebanese-first mental-health support AI with a dedicated Arabizi language layer, evidence-informed therapeutic behavior, a deterministic safety system, and an honest design that points people back toward skills, relationships, and professional help when appropriate.
about.team.title: Clinical roadmap
about.team.drFadi.name: Clinical review
about.team.drFadi.bio: The MVP's therapeutic behavior is encoded through evidence-informed guidance and structured evaluation. The production roadmap includes formal review with Lebanese mental-health professionals before presenting My Hayat as clinically validated.
about.team.drSafia.name: Language quality
about.team.drSafia.bio: The language layer is being built from native-speaker corrections, Lebanese Arabizi research, and carefully filtered public-language data. Native-speaker review remains part of the evaluation loop.
about.values.title: How it's built
about.values.1.title: Language as infrastructure
about.values.1.desc: Lebanese Arabizi is a generation system, not a translation toggle. Recognition vocabulary is separated from trusted generation forms.
about.values.2.title: Clinical structure, honest limits
about.values.2.desc: CBT/DBT/ACT-informed psychoeducation and conversation rules, with explicit boundaries about what the system can and cannot do.
about.values.3.title: Safety outside the model
about.values.3.desc: Deterministic safety classification, model routing, and output validation — not a single crisis paragraph in a prompt.
about.values.4.title: Progress over dependency
about.values.4.desc: Listening is allowed. Endless engagement is not the objective. The goal is to help people understand their patterns and get back to their lives.
howItWorks.title: You talk naturally.
howItWorks.titleHighlight: My Hayat does the translation work internally.
howItWorks.subtitle: Say it the way you would text it. The system figures out the rest.
howItWorks.step1.title: Say it the way you'd text it
howItWorks.step1.desc: Arabic, English, Arabizi, or the mix you actually use. No special format required.
howItWorks.step2.title: The system figures out what the moment needs
howItWorks.step2.desc: Safety, language, and context are processed before generation. Dialect failures and reasoning leaks are caught before you see the reply.
howItWorks.step3.title: The reply is checked before you see it
howItWorks.step3.desc: A quality gate buffers output and retries on a different model if validation fails. Repeated failures fall back to conservative wording.
howItWorks.step4.title: The conversation should lead somewhere
howItWorks.step4.desc: A useful question, a clearer pattern, a practical tool, or a reason to involve a human. Not an infinite loop.
howItWorks.personas.title: Illustrative scenarios
howItWorks.persona1.name: Scenario A
howItWorks.persona1.story: Someone writing mostly Arabizi with English clinical terms mixed in, asking about anxiety before a social event. The system mirrors the mix and responds in the same register.
howItWorks.persona2.name: Scenario B
howItWorks.persona2.story: Someone switching from Arabizi to English mid-conversation. The language layer follows the current turn, not the session history.
howItWorks.persona3.name: Scenario C
howItWorks.persona3.story: Someone writing Arabic script. The system responds in Arabic script without switching to Arabizi or English.

howItWorks.security.3: Safety classification runs before the language model

pricing.faq.title: Frequently asked questions
pricing.faq.a1: No. My Hayat is a mental-health support prototype. It can help with reflection, psychoeducation, and practical coping tools, but it does not diagnose, treat, or replace a licensed professional.
pricing.faq.a2: Because language is part of the barrier. Many Lebanese conversations naturally move between Arabic, English, French, and Arabizi. My Hayat is being built for that reality rather than forcing people into formal Arabic or perfect English.
pricing.faq.q3: What happens if the AI gets the dialect wrong?
pricing.faq.a3: The language pipeline checks generated replies for known Egyptian leakage, invented forms, script mismatches, and other quality failures. A failed response is retried on a different model, and repeated failures fall back to conservative wording.
pricing.faq.a4: High-risk messages are handled by deterministic safety logic rather than relying only on a generative model. My Hayat is not an emergency service — it surfaces local crisis resources and stays present, but it is not a substitute for emergency care.
